Matt co-created a developer portal, developed cross-stack SDKs and use-case-driven documentation, and built secure, virtualized testing environments. 🐾 There were production defects on **JP Morgan Chase’s** ACCESS payments platform, including a payment-verification failure.

The specific incident was a failure in the Message Authentication Code (MAC) security layer, which let corporate users validate payment integrity before release. Matt used break-glass production access and queried live payment data through SQL to triage it. The root cause was **missing unit tests and weak error handling**. The account does not specify the outage duration, how many transactions were affected, or any financial loss.

There were also post-cutover production defects, primarily data issues carried over from the legacy platform during migration. The regional systems had different schemas, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance records. Matt ran user acceptance testing and production validation/shakeout testing, then triaged defects that emerged after cutover. The migration itself was completed without disruption to live payment operations, which is separate from saying that no defects occurred afterward.

Matt owned on-call and **Sev-1** incident response across releases, waves, and migrations. He coordinated root-cause analysis across **JP Morgan Chase**, the offshore teams in Mumbai and Bangalore, and Bottomline Technologies. While incidents were live, he ran status updates and daily leadership calls.

The broader delivery pressure was that WebSeries did not provide all the payment, security, and workflow capabilities the bank needed out of the box. Matt managed the boundary between platform configuration and custom engineering under aggressive delivery timelines. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, but the work included production incident response and post-cutover defect triage, not just the launch.

🐾 There were production defects in the **JP Morgan Chase** ACCESS payments work, including a payment-verification failure and legacy data issues after cutover.

The clearest incident was a failure in the Message Authentication Code (MAC) security layer, which let corporate users validate payment integrity before release. Matt used break-glass production access and SQL queries against live payment data to investigate. The root cause was **missing unit tests and weak error handling**. The account does not specify the incident’s duration, affected payment volume, or whether customers experienced payment delays.

A separate problem surfaced during the migration from regional payment systems. Those systems had different schemas, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance records. Production defects emerged after cutover, primarily **data issues carried over from the legacy platform**. Matt ran UAT and production validation/shakeout testing and triaged those defects during rollout.

The wider integration work also involved different message formats, protocols, and regulatory requirements across **12 countries**, under aggressive delivery timelines. Matt repeatedly owned **Sev-1 incident response** across releases and migrations, coordinating root-cause analysis among the NY team, engineers in Mumbai and Bangalore, and Bottomline Technologies. While incidents were live, he ran status updates and daily leadership calls.

The distinction is that production defects occurred, but the migration was completed **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. There is no documented incident-by-incident recovery timeline or quantified customer impact in these accounts.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment engines to cross-border workflows and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation. The bank needed more than an out-of-box deployment of Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries: each payment type had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Regional legacy systems also had different client configurations, entitlement structures, and transaction histories.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources. He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. The work included payment-type-specific permissions, Message Authentication Code verification, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. Corporate treasurers could initiate cross-currency payments with embedded rate visibility, rather than manage those functions through separate platforms. He also led payments data migration while preserving compliance traceability, with **zero disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, working with the FX team on real-time currency conversion and transaction visibility. His scope included automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and bulk processing. The deliverable was a complete implementation blueprint, ready for development execution. Revised cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform offered real-time controls and flexible APIs, but clients lacked SDKs, coherent documentation, and a sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed cross-stack SDKs, and introduced secure sandbox and virtualized testing environments so developers could test earlier without downstream dependencies. He also used a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather feedback. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time fell, and the team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

answer_md:
🐾 The degree title and the work Matt has done are separate facts.

Matt has a Master's degree in Information Technology from **American InterContinental University**. Information Technology is a recognized Computer Science-related discipline, and a Master's degree exceeds a Bachelor's. That is not the same as holding a degree titled Computer Science.

His work includes software engineering, application modernization, and solution architecture. At **Cendant Mortgage**, underwriters and loan officers worked in a mainframe green-screen application. The replacement required a web front end, executable underwriting workflows, and an Oracle database layer. At **AT&T**, a network engineering platform needed integration agreements and detailed technical designs across distributed development teams. These were implementation responsibilities, not just advisory assignments.

At **Cendant Mortgage**, Matt built the JSP and MVC front end, configured and maintained the TIBCO process layer, and modeled credit report requests, verification flows, and conditional routing to manager approval. He also found and corrected flaws in the math and logic of Oracle stored procedures calculating risk factors. Underwriters moved to a web application, with the underwriting workflow executing in a process engine.

At **AT&T**, Matt designed enhancements using .NET, C#, SQL Server, and ESRI APIs. He defined integration agreements for **3** systems, reviewed offshore-delivered code, and traveled to Hyderabad to transition technical designs and resolve development issues. Enhancements delivered without architectural rework between phases.

He also taught entry-level Enterprise Java at **American InterContinental University** alongside full-time consulting work. Students built a working Java web application with persistence and session state, progressing through servlets, JDBC, MySQL, JSP, JavaBeans, and MVC.

If your requirement is specifically a CS-titled degree, his degree does not meet that wording. If your concern is whether he has built and reviewed software, those are examples of work he performed.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt leads.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, he established a “permit to fail” environment for teams that had avoided risks because they feared blame. He organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail intentionally: teams used those results to challenge assumptions before committing to costly builds.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the dashboard. He audited the code and tests, exposed gaps in the backlog, and rebuilt stories with defined scenarios and a definition of done. He brought in test-driven development experts to work alongside engineers, using coding katas, practice sessions, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

He also assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability, rather than separate role silos. Teams used pair programming, collaborative coding, and regular retrospectives. Across his leadership work at the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. In one engagement, Matt took accountability, but the tester still bore an individual consequence.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client, with development, QA, UAT, and production environments. The program was under delivery pressure, and offshore teams were executing test cycles. His responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup, but he relied on inherited documentation rather than verifying IAM configuration, environment boundaries, and downstream access controls.

He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not verify that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. Communications went to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team model and emphasis on test-driven development did not initially produce the quality Matt expected.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly, including the problems in the backlog.

Engineers redid the code and test cases, supported by boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing through an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

Defect rates dropped, and **Norfolk Southern** stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. The initial setup had left engineers working from vague stories while leadership relied on coverage numbers. Matt changed both the requirements and the day-to-day coaching, not just the reporting.

answer_md:
🐾 There’s an example where Matt’s “permit to fail” principle did not protect someone from consequences.

On a global platform modernization for a financial services client, Matt was the tech lead responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. He relied on inherited documentation and assumed the identity and access management controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations were correct.

He did not verify those assumptions. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer data had been masked, or implement compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. In Matt’s words, it was “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

His stated change afterward was specific: IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became “day-one leadership responsibilities” in his delivery approach. His account does not claim that taking accountability reversed the tester’s removal.

🐾 Here’s the ownership Matt actually held.

The stories don’t establish that Matt is better than someone who stayed in-house. They do document more than project delivery: at **Accenture**, Matt built and ran the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers over **4 years**, with full P&L accountability, budget and cost management, hiring, performance evaluation, promotions, compensation allocation, and remediation decisions.

The organization grew from a **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners**. The challenge was not just staffing engagements. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native experience, and the deliberately flat organization had no managers sitting on daily delivery teams. Matt had to build the machinery for developing people and evaluating their work without adding management layers.

He used hands-on pairing auditions rather than relying only on interviews, and made the final hiring decision on every offer. Practitioners progressed through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model. For performance evaluation, practice leads gathered evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors rather than relying on a director’s impressions. At **Accenture**, clients wanted to move beyond waterfall and feature factories, but the organization lacked a scalable model for modern product engineering. answer_md:
🐾 Yes. Matt worked as a Director with a **Major U.S. Health System** through **Accenture** from May to September **2023**, on AI-powered chronic disease management and responsible AI governance.

The health system had an existing condition management application supporting diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease, but care was largely reactive, with limited real-time patient insights. Matt led an initiative to add AI-powered capabilities, starting with diabetes management. He designed and implemented a data lake, machine learning pipeline, LLM-driven chat, and mobile components using data from electronic medical records, glucometers, activity trackers, and other devices. His team delivered a working MVP in **16 weeks**, built as an extensible foundation rather than a throwaway proof of concept. Patients in the pilot received real-time health insights and personalized recommendations through the mobile app.

The CIO also raised concerns about HIPAA compliance and patient privacy. Matt brought together legal, compliance, IT security, data science, and clinical representatives to establish policies and operational oversight. He implemented anonymization, encryption, differential privacy, continuous monitoring, and auditing, and regularly updated the CIO and executive team during the pilot.

The pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance. Matt trained healthcare teams to interpret AI-generated insights, and clinical teams incorporated those insights into treatment planning. The executive team approved consideration of broader AI implementation.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt got it wrong.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on assumptions rather than verifying the configuration. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes corporate payment engines, cross-border workflow design, legacy migration, and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, the ACCESS Next Generation portal needed payment capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Each payment type had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries. Matt led a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and the bank, spending **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices.

Rather than treating ACCESS as a standard platform deployment, he managed the build-versus-configure boundary and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. He implemented Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and integration with centralized transaction monitoring. His responsibilities also included production incident response and diagnosing payment defects through live SQL queries.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. In the payments migration workstream, Matt coordinated legacy data mapping, verification, and compliance dashboards. Client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories were consolidated with **zero disruption** to live payment processing.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, partnering with the FX team on real-time currency conversion and transaction visibility. He also designed bulk processing, recurring payments, and Interac e-Transfer workflows. The deliverable was an implementation blueprint, with revised cutoff processes reducing wire-transfer delays.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox. Matt’s work addressed those integration barriers through Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, secure sandbox testing, and environment virtualization. The team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated the portal through a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months**; the developer-experience work delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond the team’s commitment.

He brings product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, using user research, rapid testing, and thin-slice, production-ready delivery rather than waiting for polished requirements.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what happened at **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s team was modernizing the railroad’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A few months in, just as the pandemic forced everyone into remote work, the client reported rising defects. The team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns reached both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure in front of both groups rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation, then writing tests after the code. The backlog also contributed: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done, leaving no clear way to test them.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers and redo the code and tests. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression, supported by boot camps, coding katas, and practice learning sessions. He also restructured agile ceremonies so stakeholders, developers, and product managers worked from shared requirements.

After the experts left, Matt reinforced the practices through daily pair rotation, test cases written before implementation, and checks at standup. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners rather than receiving instructions alone.

Defect rates dropped, the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and the failure mode did not recur after the outside experts went home.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, the client reported rising defects, even though the team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done, leaving no clear way to test them.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers. Instead of issuing a process mandate, he used boot camps, coding katas, practice sessions, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression.

After the immediate correction, he reinforced the daily workflow. Engineers rotated pairs, built test cases before engineering the solution, and checked that sequence at standup. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners so the practices would not depend on visiting experts or Matt’s direct oversight.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Pairing and test-first remained the team’s default after the experts left, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization from **November 2019** to **September 2023**, the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. The railroad’s mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The work also faced resistance to product delivery, waterfall expectations, and the shift to remote work during the pandemic.

Matt led event storming and domain-driven design sessions to map embedded business functions. Rather than replace the mainframe outright, his team kept it as the system of record while building APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. The architecture also used asynchronous messaging and anti-corruption layers for legacy integration.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management staff into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace. They moved from personas and user flows to prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

The engagement also hit a quality crisis: defects were rising despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code and vague backlog stories. He brought in TDD experts, rebuilt testable stories, and reinforced test-first work through rotating pairs, coding katas, and daily workflow checks. A CIC Academy course ran twice monthly over **6 months**, while pairing spread scarce domain knowledge and taught client contributors Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts.

The MVP launched covering **95% of its targeted use cases**, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation began catching fallout proactively rather than waiting for customer calls. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and pairing and test-first practices held after the outside experts left.

🐾 Here’s a closer look at the modernization and the quality crisis inside it.

Components moved incrementally using the Strangler pattern, with API gateways and anti-corruption layers maintaining interoperability.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership. A bottom-up audit found an engineer writing tests after code built from his own interpretation. Vague backlog stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to redo code and tests alongside the team. He reinforced test-first through coding katas, daily rotating pairs, and standup checks. Stories entered sprints only when testable and small enough for a **one-week** iteration.

When the client wanted more tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace through weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation began notifying trading partners proactively. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and pairing and test-first remained in place after the outside experts left.

🐾 Here’s the deeper look at the live-system migration and the changes in how the teams worked.

At **Norfolk Southern**, modernization could not depend on a big-bang cutover. Scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash still ran on the **1970s** mainframe. Clerks manually shepherded waybill and rating fallout through green screens, and malformed incoming EDI data could cause pricing errors downstream. Meanwhile, client leaders wanted tangible progress, account leadership expected waterfall delivery, and the CIC team was learning a new working model during the transition to remote work.

Matt started by mapping the embedded business functions with cross-workstream teams through domain-driven design and event storming. Delivery gates covered order management, booking, credit, service fulfillment, planning, billing/invoice, and accounts receivable. A reporting engine tracked progress through those domains.

Rather than replacing everything at once, the teams routed traffic to microservices incrementally using the Strangler pattern. API gateways and anti-corruption layers maintained interoperability. Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD supported the new services. Change data capture synchronized the mainframe with CockroachDB, while reconciliation reports checked for lost data or functionality. Synchronization itself required investigation: the client’s **2 environments** were inconsistent, and some captured changes initially could not be explained by either side.

When stakeholders grew restless, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub. They co-created the Shipper Revenue System workspace, moving from personas and user flows to prototypes validated in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. Billing clerks and shippers could audit and clean malformed waybill data before it caused downstream errors.

The working practices also met resistance. Matt addressed objections to pair programming by letting the client experience it firsthand. Thin-stretched domain experts paired through an “I do, we do, you do” progression, then rotated knowledge through the team. His **2-day** CIC Academy course ran twice monthly over **6 months**.

The MVP covered **95% of targeted use cases**, captured real orders, and fed clean data to the mainframe. EDI validation proactively notified trading partners of fallout. Delivery expanded to **3 balanced teams**, with **1 team** beginning transition to Monterrey.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The CIC stories describe growth from a **10-person pilot to 150+ practitioners**, rather than a starting team of **4**. At **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, the challenge was not just hiring: many new joiners lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Matt also needed to run hiring, development, evaluation, and promotions without adding layers of managers who did not work alongside the teams.

He built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interview participation was capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery time and avoid burning out interviewers.

New hires moved into tailored enablement and round-robin pairing with experienced practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” progressing from guided work to independent delivery. Skills matrices, mentoring, weekly peer-led demos, and career-development conversations continued after onboarding.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to him. Balanced teams combined product, design, and engineering, with experienced engineering anchors inside the teams rather than another management layer. Monday allocation reviews matched practitioners to client work and internal learning based on needs, skills, and location.

Because managers did not sit on daily teams, evaluations drew on recent pairing partners, product managers, and anchors. Matt ran monthly feedback sessions and facilitated promotion calibration, so advancement depended on evidence from daily teammates rather than visibility to a boss.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with **near-zero attrition in the first 2 years** and multiple hires promoted.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes Execution & Delivery at **JP Morgan Chase** and developer onboarding for **American Express**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different formats, protocols, entitlement structures, and compliance records. The bank was building ACCESS Next Generation on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform, but its requirements went well beyond the out-of-box offering.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources in the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline’s engineers in Portsmouth, coordinating with bank stakeholders in Chicago and NY/NJ. He determined where platform configuration ended and custom engineering was required.

Matt designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, along with payment verification and payment-type-specific permissions. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. He coordinated migration with compliance teams, preserved client configurations and transaction histories, and owned production incident response, including cross-team root-cause analysis and daily leadership calls.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients across 180+ countries**. The legacy-system migration completed without disruption to live payment operations.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform faced a different obstacle: missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, dependency bottlenecks, and no sandbox made integration difficult. Matt brought business and technical stakeholders into North Star and Discovery and Framing workshops, then coordinated stable virtualized testing environments with client teams.

The work included Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, a secure sandbox, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points**.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The CIC growth story starts with a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**, and reaches **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design. At **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, growing client demand meant hiring people who often lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, while continuing to deliver client work.

Matt built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live client briefs, user stories, or wireframes. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process added **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interview participation was capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** so recruiting did not consume delivery time or burn out interviewers.

New hires moved through tailored enablement and round-robin pairing with experienced practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” progressing from guided work to independent delivery. Peer-led tech talks, practice forums, and learning within live client projects continued after onboarding.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to him. Experienced engineers served as team anchors without adding another management layer. Weekly allocation reviews matched people to engagements and internal learning work based on skills, need, and location.

Because managers did not sit beside practitioners daily, performance reviews drew on recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors. Career-level expectations, regular development conversations, and promotion calibration gave practitioners explicit paths for advancement.

He ran a deliberately flat organization through **11 to 13 direct-report practice and client leads**, made every final hiring decision, facilitated promotion calibration, and allocated compensation budgets. The stories do not establish ownership of a long-running internal developer platform with production SLOs, on-call operations, incident management, or platform adoption targets. answer_md:
🐾 Matt has worked on commerce technology, though his documented experience is not a direct engagement for a retailer.

At **Wellfound Technology**, Matt worked on **Sparkfly** from late **2000** through **2001**. The business began as an employee discount program, and its founder was bringing in customers faster than the platform could carry them. Matt joined as a developer and grew into the lead, leading **4 developers** while continuing to write production code and taking ownership of the architecture and data layer.

He built the commerce path end to end: catalog search and genre browse, product details with pricing and savings calculations, cross-sell to related titles and authors, a cart handling multiple item types, and checkout. He also built the Books, Music, and Video channels, including channel-specific search, browse taxonomies, and editorially curated promotional slots. Personalization included interest taxonomies, geographic settings for local merchants, and user-controlled channel visibility.

When the original JSP-only architecture became fragile and slow, Matt learned the MVC pattern and refactored the live product onto servlets and beans. He worked alongside the founder, with the customer list growing while the team built.

The commerce, personalization, content, and administrative capabilities shipped as an integrated portal. **Sparkfly** later evolved into the retail technology platform it is today, but Matt’s work was on its earlier employee-discount and commerce platform.

answer_md:
🐾 Here are Matt’s core themes, with examples from his work.

**Execution & Delivery.** Matt builds products, platforms, and the organizations that deliver them. At **Accenture**, he built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, delivering **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**. CIC reported **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments through test-driven development and automated pipelines.

**Org & Working-Model Transformation.** Matt moved teams from waterfall and siloed handoffs to iterative development and balanced teams combining product, engineering, and design. He adapted pair programming, hypothesis-driven design, and Lean XP for enterprise security, compliance, and legacy systems.

**Talent & Enablement.** Matt built competency frameworks, assessed individual and team gaps, and prescribed targeted coaching across product management, agile, DevOps, and modern engineering. He used “I do, we do, you do,” live coding, immersive labs, and practice on real client work rather than off-the-shelf training.

**Strategic & Advisory.** At **RBC**, Matt assessed whether Bottomline WebSeries could meet corporate banking requirements. Code reviews, architectural heat maps, and gap/fit analysis identified missing modularity before further investment. The bank redirected resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

**Risk & Responsible Tech.** At **HSBC**, fragmented mortgage systems and manual processes created compliance risk following a federal settlement. Matt conducted assessment workshops and developed a target-state architecture using Mortgage Cadence and Black Knight, replacing compliance-risk manual processes with automated workflows.

**Emerging Tech.** Matt’s work includes cloud-native systems, AWS architecture, and reusable architectural patterns and reference implementations for modern product engineering.

**Professional Narrative.** Matt’s career runs from Software Engineer to Solution Architect to Director to Cloud Innovation Center Leader. His own description is: “Matt builds what’s next, modernizes what’s not, and grows teams along the way.”

🐾 Matt’s work spans seven core themes.

**Execution & Delivery** and **Org & Working-Model Transformation** sit at the center. At **Accenture**, clients wanted to move from waterfall to iterative development, from feature factories to customer-centric product development, and from siloed teams to balanced teams. Coaching needs varied across product management, agile, DevOps, and modern engineering. Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, adapted Lean XP for enterprise complexity, and embedded pair programming, test-driven development, and automated pipelines. The centers grew from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**.

He used dojo, lab, immersive, and self-paced interventions, including an “I do, we do, you do” progression on real-world challenges. The competency frameworks became the diagnostic tool for coaching interventions across CloudFirst.

**Emerging Tech** covers experimentation before large commitments. At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, clients wanted to explore new technologies but lacked clear adoption strategies. Matt led design thinking workshops and built working prototypes or MVPs, compressing validation cycles from months to weeks.

**Strategic & Advisory** covers decisions about what to build or buy. At **RBC**, Matt assessed whether WebSeries could meet the bank’s corporate banking requirements. Code reviews, architectural heat maps, and gap/fit analysis identified missing modularity before significant spend was committed. The bank redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

**Risk & Responsible Tech** covers privacy, security, and governance within delivery. At a **Major U.S. Health System**, Matt brought legal, compliance, IT security, data science, and clinical teams together, implemented privacy-preserving architecture, and established continuous monitoring and auditing. The pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance.

**Professional Narrative** covers Matt’s account of his career: from engineer to Director, building products, platforms, and teams. His own phrasing is: “Matt builds what’s next, modernizes what’s not, and grows teams along the way.”

🐾 Here’s what connects Matt’s work across clients.

Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement recur across his work. At **Norfolk Southern**, silos across product teams and leadership slowed cloud modernization. At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt created a shared requirements backlog, negotiated trade-offs across regional leaders, and established dependency tracking across **7 workstreams**. Across the Cloud Innovation Centers, he brought product management, design, and engineering into balanced teams, embedded test-driven development and automated pipelines, and documented reusable playbooks. Coaching used real project work rather than concepts alone.

The outcomes included delivery and continued client ownership. **JP Morgan Chase’s** Salesforce platform launched on schedule across **12 countries** and **3 regions**, with no scope renegotiations mid-flight. **Norfolk Southern** contributors gained the skills to support and manage the application after **Accenture** rolled off. Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**. Those centers delivered **30+ product engagements**, achieved **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments, and contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business** through delivery excellence and client relationships.

He rebuilt the backlog and brought in practitioners to pair with engineers. Daily pair rotation subsequently spread domain knowledge, and the failure mode did not recur after the experts left.

Talent & Enablement appears alongside delivery. At **AT&T**, Matt mentored junior developers through code reviews, unit testing, and training materials. They became independent contributors, and the Service Broker shipped with **zero critical defects**. At **Accenture**, he built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **zero to 150+ practitioners**, with training across product, design, and engineering.

Risk & Responsible Tech appears in the implementation details. At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt delivered payment verification, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. The global payments gateway gave corporate treasurers a single entry point across **12 countries**, replacing separate regional payment systems.

For Strategic & Advisory and Emerging Tech work, Matt used client workshops, research partnerships, and capability showcases rather than methodology presentations alone. The CIC generated **\$100M+** in repeatable business through delivery reputation and trusted relationships.
